Denis is a news writer for Collider with close to five years of experience in the industry. He has analyzed shows across different genres, formats and styles. His favorite types of articles to write are exciting news updates and episodic deep-dives. He might say he doesn't have a favorite show, but he has watched The Wire, Shameless, The Big Bang Theory, and The Blacklist more than once. Denis is increasingly becoming focused on the global streaming arena and how media connects with audiences in various markets. Find him on X tweeting about something random that occurred to him about a TV show or the industry in general.

For the past half-decade plus, Apple TV has built its reputation as a premium entertainment destination. It has slowly risen from a fledgling streamer initially thought of as a side project for Apple to a major television and movie player. The journey has been slow but steady as the service has claimed its place in the sci-fi and thriller space. It has also drawn major awards attention and become a serious threat to the likes of Netflix and HBO.

Many Apple TV shows are considered successes thanks to engaging stories and top-tier production quality, even when the service has never revealed raw viewership numbers. The streamer also offers a variety of stories, championing both book-to-series adaptations and original ideas. Its first major hit arrived in 2020 when Ted Lasso premiered to critical and audience acclaim. But before that, shows such as The Morning Show also attracted attention with their timely stories and strong casts. This year, however, Apple TV landed its new smash hit, which has become a streaming sensation and broken records for Emmy wins and nominations.

This show was a slight departure from what Apple TV is known for, but it wasn't any less good. It blended genres to deliver a fresh, entertaining story that critics immediately recognized, earning a near-perfect 98% on Rotten Tomatoes. Viewers were not far behind, giving the dramedy a 92%. It's been months since the series Widow's Bay completed its first season, but that hasn't stopped it on streaming. Streaming rankings from FlixPatrol show the horror comedy is still one of Apple TV's most-streamed shows, ranking fifth at the time of writing. This is no minor feat for a new show with only eight episodes, as most new shows fall off a month after the season finale.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
What Is Your Biggest Horror Nightmare?
Elm Street · Chucky · Scream · The Conjuring

Four horror franchises. Four completely different ways of scaring you. One waits until you fall asleep. One makes sure nobody believes you. One is already in your group of friends. And one is in the house with your family. Answer eight quick questions about how you actually watch horror, and find out which nightmare was built for you.

Which horror scene makes you cover your eyes?
Four classic images. One of them is worse than the others for you.

ASomebody falling asleep when they really should not.
BA toy that has moved, and nobody touched it.
CA phone ringing in an empty house.
DA child talking to somebody who is not there.

You are home alone and you hear a noise. First thought?
Everybody has one. It arrives before you have decided anything.

AI am exhausted and my mind is playing tricks on me.
BSomething in this room is not where I left it.
CSomebody is in here with me.
DThis house has never felt entirely right.

Which horror movie rule would you break first?
Everybody thinks they would survive. Almost nobody actually does.

ANever fall asleep.
BNever leave it out of your sight.
CNever answer the phone.
DNever go down to the basement.

Something genuinely frightening happens. What do you do?
Not in a film. In your actual living room, tonight.

AConvince myself I imagined the whole thing.
BTell someone, and brace for them not believing me.
CWork out which person I know could be behind it.
DGet everybody in the house into one room.

How do you actually watch a horror film?
Be honest about this one. Nobody is checking.

AFine during. Wide awake at two in the morning.
BShouting at the screen that nobody is listening.
CCalling the twist out loud before it lands.
DThrough my fingers, holding on to something.

Somebody offers you serious money. Which do you still refuse?
The amount does not matter. There is one on this list you are not doing.

AFall asleep in a room I have never been in before.
BKeep an old doll on the shelf facing my bed.
CAnswer every unknown number that calls after midnight.
DSpend one night alone in a house with a history.

Which feeling stays with you a week after the film?
Good horror does not stop when the credits do.

ANot wanting to turn the bedroom light off.
BNot trusting one particular object in my house.
CLooking twice at people I have known for years.
DFeeling like something came home with me.

Something wakes you at 3am. What is the worst possibility?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your nightmare.

AThat I am still asleep, and it knows it.
BThat the thing nobody believed me about is here.
CThat somebody with a key is downstairs.
DThat something is in the doorway, watching us sleep.

The Lights Just Went Out
Your Nightmare Is…

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath
your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what
it would leave behind.
A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.
You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the
person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.
By the time somebody finally believes you, you will have handled most of it on your own.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.
Everybody is a suspect, including the person who just offered to walk you home.
The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than
personal, which is rarer than it sounds.

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
standing in the hallway.
